title: Permissions and Privileged Operations
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose of Permissions and Privileged Operations and define its core vocabulary.
Apply permissions and privileged operations in a small PowerShell example and predict its result.
Identify one relevant edge case, version constraint, or troubleshooting step.

content.intro: This lesson covers Permissions and Privileged Operations in the PowerShell learning path. It expands the supplied syllabus heading into an actionable draft with a visual, a worked example, and a short knowledge check.
content.why_it_matters: The PowerShell language is broadly portable, but providers, paths, permissions and system tools vary by operating system. Detect platform requirements explicitly and keep common logic separate from platform-specific commands; report unsupported capabilities rather than silently failing.

content_blocks.text: Start with the syllabus concepts: User identities and permissions; Administrator, root, and elevated execution; Least-privilege operation; Handling denied access predictably. content_blocks.troubleshooting: Check command availability with Get-Command, inspect values with Get-Member, consult Get-Help -Full, and verify PowerShell version/platform before assuming identical output. Do not run examples that change system state without adapting and reviewing them.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and use synthetic values. If you created test files, delete only those files within the dedicated practice folder after checking their paths.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety note
content_blocks.text: The main path targets modern PowerShell 7.6 LTS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 compatibility is labeled separately. Some providers, admin cmdlets and APIs depend on OS, module version, permissions or tenant access; the examples are static references, not proof of execution.

content.task: Try it yourself: reduce permissions and validate inputs before an action. Use synthetic data or a disposable practice folder, write down your predicted result, check it locally, and explain one boundary case.
